case_info.scenario: A 36-year-old man with no significant medical history presented with 10 weeks of recurrent fevers (temperature up to 39.5 °C), malaise, night sweats, 30-lb unintentional weight loss, and dyspnea. The patient had a COVID-19 infection 2 months before presentation. Rheumatologic and infectious workup was unrevealing, including negative HIV and hepatitis test results. Imaging was notable for hepatosplenomegaly and a likely liver hemangioma measuring 3 × 3.2 × 3.2 cm. Hospital admission laboratory values showed a hemoglobin level of 8.6 g/dL (to convert to g/L, multiply by 10) with normal white blood cell and platelet counts. Fasting triglycerides level was elevated to 404 mg/dL (to convert to mmol/L, multiply by 0.0113) and ferritin level was elevated to 1357.7 ng/dL (to convert to µg/L, multiply by 1). Fibrinogen was normal at 429 mg/dL (to convert to g/L, multiply by 0.01) and lactate dehydrogenase was minimally elevated to 291 U/L (to convert to µkat/L, multiply by 0.0167). Liver function test results were normal. Bone marrow biopsy was negative for a hematologic malignancy but showed scant hemophagocytes. Positron emission tomography–computed tomography (PET-CT) scan demonstrated splenomegaly with a maximum standardized uptake value of 4.4 (Figure 1). The spleen measured 19.5 cm on ultrasonography. Soluble CD25 level was elevated to 7657.3 pg/mL. The patient met 5 of 8 HLH-2004 diagnostic criteria. Liver biopsy demonstrated hemophagocytes only. Repeat PET-CT showed worsening splenomegaly (maximum standardized uptake value, 5.7). The patient was readmitted for further evaluation.

case_info.answer: Primary splenic diffuse large B-cell lymphoma
case_info.caption: Positron emission tomography–computed tomography, with fludeoxyglucose radiotracer administered, show diffusely increased metabolic activity of the lungs, hepatosplenomegaly, and diffuse hypermetabolic bone marrow activity.
case_info.explanation: D. Primary splenic diffuse large B-cell lymphoma Despite unrevealing bone marrow and liver biopsies, a splenic biopsy revealed large atypical lymphoid cells with irregular nuclear contour, prominent nucleoli, and a high mitotic rate (Figure 2). The cells were positive for CD20, CD19, c-Myc, and Bcl-2 and were negative for CD10, BCL6, and CD30. Ki-67 was 70%. These findings were consistent with a diagnosis of primary splenic diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (PS-DLBCL), nongerminal center subtype. Immunohistochemical staining is paramount given the broad differential diagnosis.1This patient’s presentation is consistent with an aggressive lymphoma given the rapid progression of his symptoms, making indolent lymphomas like follicular lymphoma and marginal zone lymphoma less likely. Chronic active Epstein-Barr viral infection can present with recurrent fevers and hepatosplenomegaly, along with hepatitis, lymphadenopathy, and pancytopenia. This patient’s Epstein-Barr viral load was negative. Chemotherapy with rituximab, cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, vincristine, and prednisone (R-CHOP) was initiated with resolution of his fevers, and improvement in his ferritin from more than 50 000 ng/mL at the time of treatment initiation to 4301 ng/mL 3 weeks later. Due to prolonged antecedent steroid use, his course was complicated by invasive fungal sinusitis requiring multiple surgical debridements. PS-DLBCL comprises less than 1% of non-Hodgkin lymphomas and often presents with nonspecific symptoms.1In patients with malignant neoplasm–associated HLH, lymphoma is the most common underlying diagnosis.2Findings such as fever, cytopenias, hepatosplenomegaly, and elevated inflammatory markers can be seen in both HLH and PS-DLBCL resulting in a diagnostic challenge. Although the association between the 2 is infrequently described, distinguishing between HLH and PS-DLBCL may necessitate repeated biopsies of involved sites.3,4The presence of splenomegaly on imaging can result in a broad differential diagnosis which is a further challenge in prompt recognition of PS-DLBCL.5In cases of unexplained splenomegaly where neither bone marrow biopsy nor peripheral blood studies reveal the presence of a neoplasm, splenic tissue should be obtained. One study demonstrated that among patients diagnosed with primary splenic lymphoma, diffuse large B-cell lymphoma was the most common histologic finding.6Minimally invasive diagnostic procedures are safe and effective methods for diagnosing splenic lymphoma.7,8A meta-analysis of patients who underwent percutaneous needle biopsy of the spleen showed a major complication rate of 2.2%, which decreased to 1.3% when biopsies with needles larger than 18 gauge were removed from analysis.8 The current treatment for PS-DLBCL remains R-CHOP for 6 cycles.9A study showed that patients with PS-DLBCL who receive chemotherapy along with a splenectomy have significantly prolonged short-term overall and cancer-specific survival rates compared to those who only received chemotherapy; however, there was no significant difference in long-term survival rates.10Our patient remains in remission 6 months following completion of R-CHOP for 6 cycles, with no recurrence of invasive fungal sinusitis after serial debridements and a prolonged antifungal course. This case highlights the diagnostic complexities of PS-DLBCL stemming from initial nonspecific radiographic findings and hyperinflammatory symptoms, along with potential iatrogenic complications with a delay in diagnosis. A high degree of clinical suspicion is required to ensure clinicians consider this rare diagnosis when evaluating a patient with splenomegaly and persistent fevers.

   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and

     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.

case_info.answer: Primary splenic diffuse large B-cell lymphoma
case_info.caption: Positron emission tomography–computed tomography, with fludeoxyglucose radiotracer administered, show diffusely increased metabolic activity of the lungs, hepatosplenomegaly, and diffuse hypermetabolic bone marrow activity.
case_info.explanation: D. Primary splenic diffuse large B-cell lymphoma Despite unrevealing bone marrow and liver biopsies, a splenic biopsy revealed large atypical lymphoid cells with irregular nuclear contour, prominent nucleoli, and a high mitotic rate (Figure 2). The cells were positive for CD20, CD19, c-Myc, and Bcl-2 and were negative for CD10, BCL6, and CD30. Ki-67 was 70%. These findings were consistent with a diagnosis of primary splenic diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (PS-DLBCL), nongerminal center subtype. Immunohistochemical staining is paramount given the broad differential diagnosis.1This patient’s presentation is consistent with an aggressive lymphoma given the rapid progression of his symptoms, making indolent lymphomas like follicular lymphoma and marginal zone lymphoma less likely. Chronic active Epstein-Barr viral infection can present with recurrent fevers and hepatosplenomegaly, along with hepatitis, lymphadenopathy, and pancytopenia. This patient’s Epstein-Barr viral load was negative. Chemotherapy with rituximab, cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, vincristine, and prednisone (R-CHOP) was initiated with resolution of his fevers, and improvement in his ferritin from more than 50 000 ng/mL at the time of treatment initiation to 4301 ng/mL 3 weeks later. Due to prolonged antecedent steroid use, his course was complicated by invasive fungal sinusitis requiring multiple surgical debridements. PS-DLBCL comprises less than 1% of non-Hodgkin lymphomas and often presents with nonspecific symptoms.1In patients with malignant neoplasm–associated HLH, lymphoma is the most common underlying diagnosis.2Findings such as fever, cytopenias, hepatosplenomegaly, and elevated inflammatory markers can be seen in both HLH and PS-DLBCL resulting in a diagnostic challenge. Although the association between the 2 is infrequently described, distinguishing between HLH and PS-DLBCL may necessitate repeated biopsies of involved sites.3,4The presence of splenomegaly on imaging can result in a broad differential diagnosis which is a further challenge in prompt recognition of PS-DLBCL.5In cases of unexplained splenomegaly where neither bone marrow biopsy nor peripheral blood studies reveal the presence of a neoplasm, splenic tissue should be obtained. One study demonstrated that among patients diagnosed with primary splenic lymphoma, diffuse large B-cell lymphoma was the most common histologic finding.6Minimally invasive diagnostic procedures are safe and effective methods for diagnosing splenic lymphoma.7,8A meta-analysis of patients who underwent percutaneous needle biopsy of the spleen showed a major complication rate of 2.2%, which decreased to 1.3% when biopsies with needles larger than 18 gauge were removed from analysis.8 The current treatment for PS-DLBCL remains R-CHOP for 6 cycles.9A study showed that patients with PS-DLBCL who receive chemotherapy along with a splenectomy have significantly prolonged short-term overall and cancer-specific survival rates compared to those who only received chemotherapy; however, there was no significant difference in long-term survival rates.10Our patient remains in remission 6 months following completion of R-CHOP for 6 cycles, with no recurrence of invasive fungal sinusitis after serial debridements and a prolonged antifungal course. This case highlights the diagnostic complexities of PS-DLBCL stemming from initial nonspecific radiographic findings and hyperinflammatory symptoms, along with potential iatrogenic complications with a delay in diagnosis. A high degree of clinical suspicion is required to ensure clinicians consider this rare diagnosis when evaluating a patient with splenomegaly and persistent fevers.

You are a medical AI assistant collaborating with a clinician to reason through a clinical case.
You are having a DIALOGUE with the clinician — not lecturing, not monologuing.

[Core Objective]
Help the clinician reach the correct diagnosis or management decision through structured deliberation.

[Interaction Guidelines]
1. **Collaboration**: Work as a partner. Build upon the clinician's correct reasoning.
2. **Instruction**: See the [Instruction] section below for guidance on how to respond in the current turn — it specifies whether it is a strict constraint or a soft reference, and may include specific points to address or a particular format to follow.
3. **Safety First**: Patient safety overrides politeness. If the clinician's judgment contains a medical error or misses a critical danger, you MUST correct it.
4. **Concise turns**: Each turn should be 2–4 sentences. Do not produce long lists or procedure walkthroughs.

[Case]
A 36-year-old man with no significant medical history presented with 10 weeks of recurrent fevers (temperature up to 39.5 °C), malaise, night sweats, 30-lb unintentional weight loss, and dyspnea. The patient had a COVID-19 infection 2 months before presentation. Rheumatologic and infectious workup was unrevealing, including negative HIV and hepatitis test results. Imaging was notable for hepatosplenomegaly and a likely liver hemangioma measuring 3 × 3.2 × 3.2 cm. Hospital admission laboratory values showed a hemoglobin level of 8.6 g/dL (to convert to g/L, multiply by 10) with normal white blood cell and platelet counts. Fasting triglycerides level was elevated to 404 mg/dL (to convert to mmol/L, multiply by 0.0113) and ferritin level was elevated to 1357.7 ng/dL (to convert to µg/L, multiply by 1). Fibrinogen was normal at 429 mg/dL (to convert to g/L, multiply by 0.01) and lactate dehydrogenase was minimally elevated to 291 U/L (to convert to µkat/L, multiply by 0.0167). Liver function test results were normal. Bone marrow biopsy was negative for a hematologic malignancy but showed scant hemophagocytes. Positron emission tomography–computed tomography (PET-CT) scan demonstrated splenomegaly with a maximum standardized uptake value of 4.4 (Figure 1). The spleen measured 19.5 cm on ultrasonography. Soluble CD25 level was elevated to 7657.3 pg/mL. The patient met 5 of 8 HLH-2004 diagnostic criteria. Liver biopsy demonstrated hemophagocytes only. The patient started taking empirical dexamethasone, 10 mg/m2, for possible hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH) with resolution of fevers. Weeks later, while tapering corticosteroids, the patient deteriorated with hypotension, persistent fevers, and hypoxemia. Repeat PET-CT showed worsening splenomegaly (maximum standardized uptake value, 5.7). The patient was readmitted for further evaluation.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

case_info.answer: Primary splenic diffuse large B-cell lymphoma
case_info.caption: Positron emission tomography–computed tomography, with fludeoxyglucose radiotracer administered, show diffusely increased metabolic activity of the lungs, hepatosplenomegaly, and diffuse hypermetabolic bone marrow activity.
case_info.explanation: D. Primary splenic diffuse large B-cell lymphoma Despite unrevealing bone marrow and liver biopsies, a splenic biopsy revealed large atypical lymphoid cells with irregular nuclear contour, prominent nucleoli, and a high mitotic rate (Figure 2). The cells were positive for CD20, CD19, c-Myc, and Bcl-2 and were negative for CD10, BCL6, and CD30. Ki-67 was 70%. These findings were consistent with a diagnosis of primary splenic diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (PS-DLBCL), nongerminal center subtype. Immunohistochemical staining is paramount given the broad differential diagnosis.1This patient’s presentation is consistent with an aggressive lymphoma given the rapid progression of his symptoms, making indolent lymphomas like follicular lymphoma and marginal zone lymphoma less likely. Chronic active Epstein-Barr viral infection can present with recurrent fevers and hepatosplenomegaly, along with hepatitis, lymphadenopathy, and pancytopenia. This patient’s Epstein-Barr viral load was negative. Chemotherapy with rituximab, cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, vincristine, and prednisone (R-CHOP) was initiated with resolution of his fevers, and improvement in his ferritin from more than 50 000 ng/mL at the time of treatment initiation to 4301 ng/mL 3 weeks later. Due to prolonged antecedent steroid use, his course was complicated by invasive fungal sinusitis requiring multiple surgical debridements. PS-DLBCL comprises less than 1% of non-Hodgkin lymphomas and often presents with nonspecific symptoms.1In patients with malignant neoplasm–associated HLH, lymphoma is the most common underlying diagnosis.2Findings such as fever, cytopenias, hepatosplenomegaly, and elevated inflammatory markers can be seen in both HLH and PS-DLBCL resulting in a diagnostic challenge. Although the association between the 2 is infrequently described, distinguishing between HLH and PS-DLBCL may necessitate repeated biopsies of involved sites.3,4The presence of splenomegaly on imaging can result in a broad differential diagnosis which is a further challenge in prompt recognition of PS-DLBCL.5In cases of unexplained splenomegaly where neither bone marrow biopsy nor peripheral blood studies reveal the presence of a neoplasm, splenic tissue should be obtained. One study demonstrated that among patients diagnosed with primary splenic lymphoma, diffuse large B-cell lymphoma was the most common histologic finding.6Minimally invasive diagnostic procedures are safe and effective methods for diagnosing splenic lymphoma.7,8A meta-analysis of patients who underwent percutaneous needle biopsy of the spleen showed a major complication rate of 2.2%, which decreased to 1.3% when biopsies with needles larger than 18 gauge were removed from analysis.8 The current treatment for PS-DLBCL remains R-CHOP for 6 cycles.9A study showed that patients with PS-DLBCL who receive chemotherapy along with a splenectomy have significantly prolonged short-term overall and cancer-specific survival rates compared to those who only received chemotherapy; however, there was no significant difference in long-term survival rates.10Our patient remains in remission 6 months following completion of R-CHOP for 6 cycles, with no recurrence of invasive fungal sinusitis after serial debridements and a prolonged antifungal course. This case highlights the diagnostic complexities of PS-DLBCL stemming from initial nonspecific radiographic findings and hyperinflammatory symptoms, along with potential iatrogenic complications with a delay in diagnosis. A high degree of clinical suspicion is required to ensure clinicians consider this rare diagnosis when evaluating a patient with splenomegaly and persistent fevers.

case_info.caption: Positron emission tomography–computed tomography, with fludeoxyglucose radiotracer administered, show diffusely increased metabolic activity of the lungs, hepatosplenomegaly, and diffuse hypermetabolic bone marrow activity.
case_info.explanation: D. Primary splenic diffuse large B-cell lymphoma Despite unrevealing bone marrow and liver biopsies, a splenic biopsy revealed large atypical lymphoid cells with irregular nuclear contour, prominent nucleoli, and a high mitotic rate (Figure 2). The cells were positive for CD20, CD19, c-Myc, and Bcl-2 and were negative for CD10, BCL6, and CD30. Ki-67 was 70%. These findings were consistent with a diagnosis of primary splenic diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (PS-DLBCL), nongerminal center subtype. Immunohistochemical staining is paramount given the broad differential diagnosis.1This patient’s presentation is consistent with an aggressive lymphoma given the rapid progression of his symptoms, making indolent lymphomas like follicular lymphoma and marginal zone lymphoma less likely. Chronic active Epstein-Barr viral infection can present with recurrent fevers and hepatosplenomegaly, along with hepatitis, lymphadenopathy, and pancytopenia. This patient’s Epstein-Barr viral load was negative. Chemotherapy with rituximab, cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, vincristine, and prednisone (R-CHOP) was initiated with resolution of his fevers, and improvement in his ferritin from more than 50 000 ng/mL at the time of treatment initiation to 4301 ng/mL 3 weeks later. Due to prolonged antecedent steroid use, his course was complicated by invasive fungal sinusitis requiring multiple surgical debridements. PS-DLBCL comprises less than 1% of non-Hodgkin lymphomas and often presents with nonspecific symptoms.1In patients with malignant neoplasm–associated HLH, lymphoma is the most common underlying diagnosis.2Findings such as fever, cytopenias, hepatosplenomegaly, and elevated inflammatory markers can be seen in both HLH and PS-DLBCL resulting in a diagnostic challenge. Although the association between the 2 is infrequently described, distinguishing between HLH and PS-DLBCL may necessitate repeated biopsies of involved sites.3,4The presence of splenomegaly on imaging can result in a broad differential diagnosis which is a further challenge in prompt recognition of PS-DLBCL.5In cases of unexplained splenomegaly where neither bone marrow biopsy nor peripheral blood studies reveal the presence of a neoplasm, splenic tissue should be obtained. One study demonstrated that among patients diagnosed with primary splenic lymphoma, diffuse large B-cell lymphoma was the most common histologic finding.6Minimally invasive diagnostic procedures are safe and effective methods for diagnosing splenic lymphoma.7,8A meta-analysis of patients who underwent percutaneous needle biopsy of the spleen showed a major complication rate of 2.2%, which decreased to 1.3% when biopsies with needles larger than 18 gauge were removed from analysis.8 The current treatment for PS-DLBCL remains R-CHOP for 6 cycles.9A study showed that patients with PS-DLBCL who receive chemotherapy along with a splenectomy have significantly prolonged short-term overall and cancer-specific survival rates compared to those who only received chemotherapy; however, there was no significant difference in long-term survival rates.10Our patient remains in remission 6 months following completion of R-CHOP for 6 cycles, with no recurrence of invasive fungal sinusitis after serial debridements and a prolonged antifungal course. This case highlights the diagnostic complexities of PS-DLBCL stemming from initial nonspecific radiographic findings and hyperinflammatory symptoms, along with potential iatrogenic complications with a delay in diagnosis. A high degree of clinical suspicion is required to ensure clinicians consider this rare diagnosis when evaluating a patient with splenomegaly and persistent fevers.

case_info.answer: Primary splenic diffuse large B-cell lymphoma
case_info.caption: Positron emission tomography–computed tomography, with fludeoxyglucose radiotracer administered, show diffusely increased metabolic activity of the lungs, hepatosplenomegaly, and diffuse hypermetabolic bone marrow activity.
case_info.explanation: D. Primary splenic diffuse large B-cell lymphoma Despite unrevealing bone marrow and liver biopsies, a splenic biopsy revealed large atypical lymphoid cells with irregular nuclear contour, prominent nucleoli, and a high mitotic rate (Figure 2). The cells were positive for CD20, CD19, c-Myc, and Bcl-2 and were negative for CD10, BCL6, and CD30. Ki-67 was 70%. These findings were consistent with a diagnosis of primary splenic diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (PS-DLBCL), nongerminal center subtype. Immunohistochemical staining is paramount given the broad differential diagnosis.1This patient’s presentation is consistent with an aggressive lymphoma given the rapid progression of his symptoms, making indolent lymphomas like follicular lymphoma and marginal zone lymphoma less likely. Chronic active Epstein-Barr viral infection can present with recurrent fevers and hepatosplenomegaly, along with hepatitis, lymphadenopathy, and pancytopenia. This patient’s Epstein-Barr viral load was negative. Chemotherapy with rituximab, cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, vincristine, and prednisone (R-CHOP) was initiated with resolution of his fevers, and improvement in his ferritin from more than 50 000 ng/mL at the time of treatment initiation to 4301 ng/mL 3 weeks later. Due to prolonged antecedent steroid use, his course was complicated by invasive fungal sinusitis requiring multiple surgical debridements. PS-DLBCL comprises less than 1% of non-Hodgkin lymphomas and often presents with nonspecific symptoms.1In patients with malignant neoplasm–associated HLH, lymphoma is the most common underlying diagnosis.2Findings such as fever, cytopenias, hepatosplenomegaly, and elevated inflammatory markers can be seen in both HLH and PS-DLBCL resulting in a diagnostic challenge. Although the association between the 2 is infrequently described, distinguishing between HLH and PS-DLBCL may necessitate repeated biopsies of involved sites.3,4The presence of splenomegaly on imaging can result in a broad differential diagnosis which is a further challenge in prompt recognition of PS-DLBCL.5In cases of unexplained splenomegaly where neither bone marrow biopsy nor peripheral blood studies reveal the presence of a neoplasm, splenic tissue should be obtained. One study demonstrated that among patients diagnosed with primary splenic lymphoma, diffuse large B-cell lymphoma was the most common histologic finding.6Minimally invasive diagnostic procedures are safe and effective methods for diagnosing splenic lymphoma.7,8A meta-analysis of patients who underwent percutaneous needle biopsy of the spleen showed a major complication rate of 2.2%, which decreased to 1.3% when biopsies with needles larger than 18 gauge were removed from analysis.8 The current treatment for PS-DLBCL remains R-CHOP for 6 cycles.9A study showed that patients with PS-DLBCL who receive chemotherapy along with a splenectomy have significantly prolonged short-term overall and cancer-specific survival rates compared to those who only received chemotherapy; however, there was no significant difference in long-term survival rates.10Our patient remains in remission 6 months following completion of R-CHOP for 6 cycles, with no recurrence of invasive fungal sinusitis after serial debridements and a prolonged antifungal course. This case highlights the diagnostic complexities of PS-DLBCL stemming from initial nonspecific radiographic findings and hyperinflammatory symptoms, along with potential iatrogenic complications with a delay in diagnosis. A high degree of clinical suspicion is required to ensure clinicians consider this rare diagnosis when evaluating a patient with splenomegaly and persistent fevers.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.

   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and

   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule

       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."

   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.

   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.

   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a

   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.

case_info.answer: Primary splenic diffuse large B-cell lymphoma
case_info.caption: Positron emission tomography–computed tomography, with fludeoxyglucose radiotracer administered, show diffusely increased metabolic activity of the lungs, hepatosplenomegaly, and diffuse hypermetabolic bone marrow activity.
case_info.explanation: D. Primary splenic diffuse large B-cell lymphoma Despite unrevealing bone marrow and liver biopsies, a splenic biopsy revealed large atypical lymphoid cells with irregular nuclear contour, prominent nucleoli, and a high mitotic rate (Figure 2). The cells were positive for CD20, CD19, c-Myc, and Bcl-2 and were negative for CD10, BCL6, and CD30. Ki-67 was 70%. These findings were consistent with a diagnosis of primary splenic diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (PS-DLBCL), nongerminal center subtype. Immunohistochemical staining is paramount given the broad differential diagnosis.1This patient’s presentation is consistent with an aggressive lymphoma given the rapid progression of his symptoms, making indolent lymphomas like follicular lymphoma and marginal zone lymphoma less likely. Chronic active Epstein-Barr viral infection can present with recurrent fevers and hepatosplenomegaly, along with hepatitis, lymphadenopathy, and pancytopenia. This patient’s Epstein-Barr viral load was negative. Chemotherapy with rituximab, cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, vincristine, and prednisone (R-CHOP) was initiated with resolution of his fevers, and improvement in his ferritin from more than 50 000 ng/mL at the time of treatment initiation to 4301 ng/mL 3 weeks later. Due to prolonged antecedent steroid use, his course was complicated by invasive fungal sinusitis requiring multiple surgical debridements. PS-DLBCL comprises less than 1% of non-Hodgkin lymphomas and often presents with nonspecific symptoms.1In patients with malignant neoplasm–associated HLH, lymphoma is the most common underlying diagnosis.2Findings such as fever, cytopenias, hepatosplenomegaly, and elevated inflammatory markers can be seen in both HLH and PS-DLBCL resulting in a diagnostic challenge. Although the association between the 2 is infrequently described, distinguishing between HLH and PS-DLBCL may necessitate repeated biopsies of involved sites.3,4The presence of splenomegaly on imaging can result in a broad differential diagnosis which is a further challenge in prompt recognition of PS-DLBCL.5In cases of unexplained splenomegaly where neither bone marrow biopsy nor peripheral blood studies reveal the presence of a neoplasm, splenic tissue should be obtained. One study demonstrated that among patients diagnosed with primary splenic lymphoma, diffuse large B-cell lymphoma was the most common histologic finding.6Minimally invasive diagnostic procedures are safe and effective methods for diagnosing splenic lymphoma.7,8A meta-analysis of patients who underwent percutaneous needle biopsy of the spleen showed a major complication rate of 2.2%, which decreased to 1.3% when biopsies with needles larger than 18 gauge were removed from analysis.8 The current treatment for PS-DLBCL remains R-CHOP for 6 cycles.9A study showed that patients with PS-DLBCL who receive chemotherapy along with a splenectomy have significantly prolonged short-term overall and cancer-specific survival rates compared to those who only received chemotherapy; however, there was no significant difference in long-term survival rates.10Our patient remains in remission 6 months following completion of R-CHOP for 6 cycles, with no recurrence of invasive fungal sinusitis after serial debridements and a prolonged antifungal course. This case highlights the diagnostic complexities of PS-DLBCL stemming from initial nonspecific radiographic findings and hyperinflammatory symptoms, along with potential iatrogenic complications with a delay in diagnosis. A high degree of clinical suspicion is required to ensure clinicians consider this rare diagnosis when evaluating a patient with splenomegaly and persistent fevers.

1. Mental Demand
   Definition:

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before

   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also

   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple

       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams

   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied

   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of

       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule

       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."

   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of

4. Frustration

   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to

case_info.scenario: A 36-year-old man with no significant medical history presented with 10 weeks of recurrent fevers (temperature up to 39.5 °C), malaise, night sweats, 30-lb unintentional weight loss, and dyspnea. The patient had a COVID-19 infection 2 months before presentation. Rheumatologic and infectious workup was unrevealing, including negative HIV and hepatitis test results. Imaging was notable for hepatosplenomegaly and a likely liver hemangioma measuring 3 × 3.2 × 3.2 cm. Hospital admission laboratory values showed a hemoglobin level of 8.6 g/dL (to convert to g/L, multiply by 10) with normal white blood cell and platelet counts. Fasting triglycerides level was elevated to 404 mg/dL (to convert to mmol/L, multiply by 0.0113) and ferritin level was elevated to 1357.7 ng/dL (to convert to µg/L, multiply by 1). Fibrinogen was normal at 429 mg/dL (to convert to g/L, multiply by 0.01) and lactate dehydrogenase was minimally elevated to 291 U/L (to convert to µkat/L, multiply by 0.0167). Liver function test results were normal. Bone marrow biopsy was negative for a hematologic malignancy but showed scant hemophagocytes. Positron emission tomography–computed tomography (PET-CT) scan demonstrated splenomegaly with a maximum standardized uptake value of 4.4 (Figure 1). The spleen measured 19.5 cm on ultrasonography. Soluble CD25 level was elevated to 7657.3 pg/mL. The patient met 5 of 8 HLH-2004 diagnostic criteria. Liver biopsy demonstrated hemophagocytes only. The patient started taking empirical dexamethasone, 10 mg/m2, for possible hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH) with resolution of fevers. Weeks later, while tapering corticosteroids, the patient deteriorated with hypotension, persistent fevers, and hypoxemia. Repeat PET-CT showed worsening splenomegaly (maximum standardized uptake value, 5.7). The patient was readmitted for further evaluation.

case_info.answer: Primary splenic diffuse large B-cell lymphoma
case_info.caption: Positron emission tomography–computed tomography, with fludeoxyglucose radiotracer administered, show diffusely increased metabolic activity of the lungs, hepatosplenomegaly, and diffuse hypermetabolic bone marrow activity.
case_info.explanation: D. Primary splenic diffuse large B-cell lymphoma Despite unrevealing bone marrow and liver biopsies, a splenic biopsy revealed large atypical lymphoid cells with irregular nuclear contour, prominent nucleoli, and a high mitotic rate (Figure 2). The cells were positive for CD20, CD19, c-Myc, and Bcl-2 and were negative for CD10, BCL6, and CD30. Ki-67 was 70%. These findings were consistent with a diagnosis of primary splenic diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (PS-DLBCL), nongerminal center subtype. Immunohistochemical staining is paramount given the broad differential diagnosis.1This patient’s presentation is consistent with an aggressive lymphoma given the rapid progression of his symptoms, making indolent lymphomas like follicular lymphoma and marginal zone lymphoma less likely. Chronic active Epstein-Barr viral infection can present with recurrent fevers and hepatosplenomegaly, along with hepatitis, lymphadenopathy, and pancytopenia. This patient’s Epstein-Barr viral load was negative. Chemotherapy with rituximab, cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, vincristine, and prednisone (R-CHOP) was initiated with resolution of his fevers, and improvement in his ferritin from more than 50 000 ng/mL at the time of treatment initiation to 4301 ng/mL 3 weeks later. Due to prolonged antecedent steroid use, his course was complicated by invasive fungal sinusitis requiring multiple surgical debridements. PS-DLBCL comprises less than 1% of non-Hodgkin lymphomas and often presents with nonspecific symptoms.1In patients with malignant neoplasm–associated HLH, lymphoma is the most common underlying diagnosis.2Findings such as fever, cytopenias, hepatosplenomegaly, and elevated inflammatory markers can be seen in both HLH and PS-DLBCL resulting in a diagnostic challenge. Although the association between the 2 is infrequently described, distinguishing between HLH and PS-DLBCL may necessitate repeated biopsies of involved sites.3,4The presence of splenomegaly on imaging can result in a broad differential diagnosis which is a further challenge in prompt recognition of PS-DLBCL.5In cases of unexplained splenomegaly where neither bone marrow biopsy nor peripheral blood studies reveal the presence of a neoplasm, splenic tissue should be obtained. One study demonstrated that among patients diagnosed with primary splenic lymphoma, diffuse large B-cell lymphoma was the most common histologic finding.6Minimally invasive diagnostic procedures are safe and effective methods for diagnosing splenic lymphoma.7,8A meta-analysis of patients who underwent percutaneous needle biopsy of the spleen showed a major complication rate of 2.2%, which decreased to 1.3% when biopsies with needles larger than 18 gauge were removed from analysis.8 The current treatment for PS-DLBCL remains R-CHOP for 6 cycles.9A study showed that patients with PS-DLBCL who receive chemotherapy along with a splenectomy have significantly prolonged short-term overall and cancer-specific survival rates compared to those who only received chemotherapy; however, there was no significant difference in long-term survival rates.10Our patient remains in remission 6 months following completion of R-CHOP for 6 cycles, with no recurrence of invasive fungal sinusitis after serial debridements and a prolonged antifungal course. This case highlights the diagnostic complexities of PS-DLBCL stemming from initial nonspecific radiographic findings and hyperinflammatory symptoms, along with potential iatrogenic complications with a delay in diagnosis. A high degree of clinical suspicion is required to ensure clinicians consider this rare diagnosis when evaluating a patient with splenomegaly and persistent fevers.

case_info.answer: Primary splenic diffuse large B-cell lymphoma
case_info.caption: Positron emission tomography–computed tomography, with fludeoxyglucose radiotracer administered, show diffusely increased metabolic activity of the lungs, hepatosplenomegaly, and diffuse hypermetabolic bone marrow activity.
case_info.explanation: D. Primary splenic diffuse large B-cell lymphoma Despite unrevealing bone marrow and liver biopsies, a splenic biopsy revealed large atypical lymphoid cells with irregular nuclear contour, prominent nucleoli, and a high mitotic rate (Figure 2). The cells were positive for CD20, CD19, c-Myc, and Bcl-2 and were negative for CD10, BCL6, and CD30. Ki-67 was 70%. These findings were consistent with a diagnosis of primary splenic diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (PS-DLBCL), nongerminal center subtype. Immunohistochemical staining is paramount given the broad differential diagnosis.1This patient’s presentation is consistent with an aggressive lymphoma given the rapid progression of his symptoms, making indolent lymphomas like follicular lymphoma and marginal zone lymphoma less likely. Chronic active Epstein-Barr viral infection can present with recurrent fevers and hepatosplenomegaly, along with hepatitis, lymphadenopathy, and pancytopenia. This patient’s Epstein-Barr viral load was negative. Chemotherapy with rituximab, cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, vincristine, and prednisone (R-CHOP) was initiated with resolution of his fevers, and improvement in his ferritin from more than 50 000 ng/mL at the time of treatment initiation to 4301 ng/mL 3 weeks later. Due to prolonged antecedent steroid use, his course was complicated by invasive fungal sinusitis requiring multiple surgical debridements. PS-DLBCL comprises less than 1% of non-Hodgkin lymphomas and often presents with nonspecific symptoms.1In patients with malignant neoplasm–associated HLH, lymphoma is the most common underlying diagnosis.2Findings such as fever, cytopenias, hepatosplenomegaly, and elevated inflammatory markers can be seen in both HLH and PS-DLBCL resulting in a diagnostic challenge. Although the association between the 2 is infrequently described, distinguishing between HLH and PS-DLBCL may necessitate repeated biopsies of involved sites.3,4The presence of splenomegaly on imaging can result in a broad differential diagnosis which is a further challenge in prompt recognition of PS-DLBCL.5In cases of unexplained splenomegaly where neither bone marrow biopsy nor peripheral blood studies reveal the presence of a neoplasm, splenic tissue should be obtained. One study demonstrated that among patients diagnosed with primary splenic lymphoma, diffuse large B-cell lymphoma was the most common histologic finding.6Minimally invasive diagnostic procedures are safe and effective methods for diagnosing splenic lymphoma.7,8A meta-analysis of patients who underwent percutaneous needle biopsy of the spleen showed a major complication rate of 2.2%, which decreased to 1.3% when biopsies with needles larger than 18 gauge were removed from analysis.8 The current treatment for PS-DLBCL remains R-CHOP for 6 cycles.9A study showed that patients with PS-DLBCL who receive chemotherapy along with a splenectomy have significantly prolonged short-term overall and cancer-specific survival rates compared to those who only received chemotherapy; however, there was no significant difference in long-term survival rates.10Our patient remains in remission 6 months following completion of R-CHOP for 6 cycles, with no recurrence of invasive fungal sinusitis after serial debridements and a prolonged antifungal course. This case highlights the diagnostic complexities of PS-DLBCL stemming from initial nonspecific radiographic findings and hyperinflammatory symptoms, along with potential iatrogenic complications with a delay in diagnosis. A high degree of clinical suspicion is required to ensure clinicians consider this rare diagnosis when evaluating a patient with splenomegaly and persistent fevers.

[Case]
A 36-year-old man with no significant medical history presented with 10 weeks of recurrent fevers (temperature up to 39.5 °C), malaise, night sweats, 30-lb unintentional weight loss, and dyspnea. The patient had a COVID-19 infection 2 months before presentation. Rheumatologic and infectious workup was unrevealing, including negative HIV and hepatitis test results. Imaging was notable for hepatosplenomegaly and a likely liver hemangioma measuring 3 × 3.2 × 3.2 cm. Hospital admission laboratory values showed a hemoglobin level of 8.6 g/dL (to convert to g/L, multiply by 10) with normal white blood cell and platelet counts. Fasting triglycerides level was elevated to 404 mg/dL (to convert to mmol/L, multiply by 0.0113) and ferritin level was elevated to 1357.7 ng/dL (to convert to µg/L, multiply by 1). Fibrinogen was normal at 429 mg/dL (to convert to g/L, multiply by 0.01) and lactate dehydrogenase was minimally elevated to 291 U/L (to convert to µkat/L, multiply by 0.0167). Liver function test results were normal. Bone marrow biopsy was negative for a hematologic malignancy but showed scant hemophagocytes. Positron emission tomography–computed tomography (PET-CT) scan demonstrated splenomegaly with a maximum standardized uptake value of 4.4 (Figure 1). The spleen measured 19.5 cm on ultrasonography. Soluble CD25 level was elevated to 7657.3 pg/mL. The patient met 5 of 8 HLH-2004 diagnostic criteria. Liver biopsy demonstrated hemophagocytes only. The patient started taking empirical dexamethasone, 10 mg/m2, for possible hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH) with resolution of fevers. Weeks later, while tapering corticosteroids, the patient deteriorated with hypotension, persistent fevers, and hypoxemia. Repeat PET-CT showed worsening splenomegaly (maximum standardized uptake value, 5.7). The patient was readmitted for further evaluation.
